summary: Proposes a small change to how TCP grows its congestion window: base the increase on the number of previously unacknowledged bytes each acknowledgment covers, rather than adding a fixed amount per acknowledgment. This improves performance and closes a hole receivers could use to push a sender to send faster. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Appropriate Byte Counting changes how TCP increases its congestion window: the sender counts the newly acknowledged data, not just the number of acknowledgments. This reduces the effect of delayed acknowledgments and prevents a receiver from speeding growth by splitting its acknowledgments.

subtitle: A TCP congestion-window rule that counts acknowledged bytes instead of acknowledgments.

tldr.problem: Growing TCP's congestion window by counting acknowledgments can respond poorly to delayed acknowledgments and can be manipulated by a receiver that splits acknowledgments.
tldr.mechanism: Appropriate Byte Counting (ABC) bases window growth on newly acknowledged bytes and limits the increase during slow start.
tldr.outcome: The Experimental RFC recommends ABC with a one-segment limit and invites further tests of a more aggressive limit.

today: RFC 3465 is Experimental. Its conclusion recommends byte counting with a one-segment increase limit and invites further experimentation with a larger limit.

sections.title: Why Count Bytes
sections.content:
TCP's congestion window limits how much unacknowledged data a sender can have in the network. Traditional growth rules react to arriving acknowledgments, so a receiver that delays acknowledgments can make the window grow more slowly.

A receiver could also send multiple acknowledgments for small pieces of one segment. The RFC calls this ACK division: because older senders counted acknowledgments, this behavior could make the sender grow its window too quickly.
sections.plainLanguage: Counting acknowledgments can make TCP's sending limit depend on how the receiver splits its replies. ABC instead measures how much new data those replies confirm.

sections.title: How Appropriate Byte Counting Works
sections.content:
During congestion avoidance, the sender accumulates newly acknowledged bytes. When the total reaches the congestion-window value, it subtracts that value and increases the window by one sender maximum segment size (SMSS).

During slow start, the sender SHOULD increase the window by the number of previously unacknowledged bytes confirmed by an acknowledgment, capped at a limit called L. Implementations MAY use L = 2*SMSS and MUST NOT use a larger value; after a retransmission timeout, the sender MUST use L = 1*SMSS.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender grows its window according to newly confirmed data. In slow start, a limit prevents one acknowledgment from causing an unlimited increase, and the limit is lower after a retransmission timeout.

sections.title: Benefits and Costs
sections.content:
Byte counting can reduce the slow growth caused by delayed acknowledgments and can make window growth better match the amount of data sent. It also blocks ACK division from creating artificial window growth, because repeated acknowledgments for the same bytes do not count as new data.

The RFC also warns that a larger slow-start limit can create larger bursts and a modest increase in packet loss. It discusses fairness as an area for more experimentation and says the simulation results are not necessarily realistic.
sections.plainLanguage: ABC can improve growth when acknowledgments are delayed and stop ACK division from fooling the sender. A larger limit can also send data in bigger bursts and increase losses.

sections.title: Security and Recommendation
sections.content:
ABC protects against a misbehaving receiver that uses ACK division to push the sender toward an inappropriate sending rate. The RFC recommends that TCP implementations use ABC with L = 1*SMSS, which does not make TCP more aggressive than the referenced rule.

The document says that simulations of a two-segment limit showed a promising performance improvement and encourages experimentation with that setting. It is an Experimental RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC recommends byte counting with the conservative one-segment limit to resist ACK division. It treats the larger limit as an experimental option, not a settled requirement.

references.text: Allman, M., Paxson, V., and W. Stevens, "TCP Congestion Control", RFC 2581, April 1999.
